medical.title: Japanese hinoki root essential oil may support better sleep at home
medical.summary: Sleep problems are common in middle age, particularly among women in their 40s and 50s. In a new study published Sept. 1, 2026, in the Journal of Wood Science, researchers explored whether essential oils derived from Hinoki (Chamaecyparis obtusa), known as Japanese cypress, roots could help improve sleep quality. Participants reported fewer nighttime awakenings, improved morning feelings and brain-wave patterns suggesting smoother sleep onset.

medical.title: New mechanism reveals how atypical E. coli maintain their ability to infect
medical.summary: A new study shows how a type of disease-causing E. coli can quickly adapt when it loses one of its main ways of attaching to the intestine. The bacteria either change shape or make small changes to a protein that strengthens their grip on human cells. The findings help explain why these strains can still cause illness and identify a possible target for future treatments that could stop infection by preventing bacteria from attaching in the first place.

medical.title: Three studies map how superbugs evade antibiotics and spread to vulnerable patients
medical.summary: To defeat multidrug-resistant superbugs, bacterial defenses must be confronted wherever they may emerge, from basic genetic mutations in a laboratory to complex real-world transmission in hospital rooms. A new trio of studies published in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy and researched by the laboratory of Barry N. Kreiswirth, Ph.D., at the Hackensack Meridian Center for Discovery and Innovation (CDI) demonstrates how an integrated approach might yet expose and overcome these diverse survival mechanisms.

medical.title: Study reveals young-onset dementia's impact on families
medical.summary: Families caring for a loved one with young-onset dementia are facing years of uncertainty, financial strain and emotional exhaustion—with many struggling to access timely diagnosis and appropriate support—according to a new Curtin University study appearing in Health Expectations.

medical.title: Osteoporosis fractures fall by 94% in small first-in-human stem cell trial
medical.summary: Somewhere in the world, a woman over 50 will have fractured a bone by the time you finish reading this sentence due to osteoporosis, a silent bone disease that can weaken the structural integrity of the skeletal system and a person's quality of life. The disease weakens bones and makes them more likely to break because of reduced bone mineral density and bone mass, and it affects an estimated 75 million people across Europe, the USA, and Japan.

medical.title: Emergency department visits for gambling disorders nearly doubled after Ontario expanded its online gambling market
medical.summary: Emergency department (ED) visits for gambling disorders doubled following the legalization of single-event sports betting and expansion of Ontario's online gambling market, according to a new study from ICES. The increase was observed predominantly among young men.

medical.title: Study supports effectiveness of RSV preventive antibodies for infants, offers new way to monitor viral resistance
medical.summary: An analysis of more than 60,000 respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) sequences from around the world found that viral variants associated with resistance to current RSV prevention tools remain rare, according to a study published in Nature.

medical.title: New study reveals how a brain protein may influence ADHD and brain development
medical.summary: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that can affect attention, activity levels and impulse control, with symptoms often beginning in childhood and sometimes continuing into adulthood.

medical.title: Targeting Nav1.7: A new approach to long-lasting relief from nerve pain
medical.summary: Pain is a natural protective mechanism that alerts the body to actual or potential injury. But when nerves themselves are damaged, they can generate abnormal pain signals even in the absence of a new injury. This condition, known as neuropathic pain, can be persistent and difficult to treat. Medicines can sometimes provide inadequate relief or cause unwanted effects, creating a need for treatments that can reduce abnormal pain without interfering with normal pain sensation.

medical.title: Can psychedelic clinical trials be better? Researchers say yes
medical.summary: UC San Francisco researchers are weighing in on one of the biggest challenges in psychedelic science, arguing that clinical trials need more convincing placebo treatments to better measure the drugs' true effects.

medical.title: New portable blood testing device could allow patient health to be monitored at home through an app
medical.summary: King's College London spinout Algocyte has developed a small blood-testing device that connects via Bluetooth and uses AI to build a picture of an individual's health over time. The tool could be especially beneficial for patients who require regular monitoring, such as those undergoing chemotherapy, who currently rely on frequent hospital or doctor visits for blood tests.

medical.title: Hope in the Storm: Studying the Daily Fight to Live
medical.summary: Understanding and preventing suicide often focuses on why people want to die—but a Yale researcher is calling for a shift to a more constructive, humanizing starting point. Christine Cha, PhD, stresses the importance of focusing on why many people who feel suicidal keep trying to live.

medical.title: Wearable sensors accurately track knee osteoarthritis mobility
medical.summary: Knee osteoarthritis is a widespread and painful joint condition. It causes chronic pain, cartilage breakdown and trouble moving. Doctors rely on X-rays and patient surveys to track how the disease progresses. These traditional methods have a major blind spot. They do not show how a person actually moves during daily life outside a clinical exam.

medical.title: Clinical guideline on radiation therapy for bladder cancer released
medical.summary: For appropriately selected patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer, preserving the bladder can be a curative treatment option rather than removing it, according to a new clinical guideline from the American Society for Radiation Oncology (ASTRO). The recommendations support trimodal therapy as an alternative to bladder removal and provide guidance on the use of radiation therapy after surgery and for patients with metastatic or symptomatic disease. The guideline, ASTRO's first to focus specifically on radiation therapy across bladder cancer care, was published in Practical Radiation Oncology, ASTRO's clinical practice journal.

medical.title: Gut supplement shows promise against opioid-related damage in rat pups
medical.summary: New UNSW research published in Translational Psychiatry shows a gut supplement can repair opioid-related damage in rat pups, raising hopes for a future treatment for babies exposed to opioids in the womb.

medical.title: Caregivers worldwide often sacrifice their own well-being, 20 years of research further confirms
medical.summary: Caregivers of people with cancer, heart problems and other long-term illnesses report needing more psychological support but often stop short of accessing it.

medical.title: Scientists find an immune “false alarm” that may drive rapid aging
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered that some severe genetic disorders linked to rapid aging may be driven not just by damaged DNA, but by the body’s overreaction to that damage. When broken DNA fragments leak into the wrong part of a cell, an immune sensor called cGAS can mistake them for signs of a viral infection, triggering chronic inflammation and even interfering with DNA repair itself.

medical.title: ASH sets new standards for diagnosing iron deficiency
medical.summary: Iron deficiency is one of the most common health conditions in the world, but many people live with symptoms for months or years before receiving a diagnosis. To address this critical unmet need, the American Society of Hematology (ASH) issued new clinical guidance to improve how iron deficiency is recognized and diagnosed across key populations, including adults, young children, menstruating and pregnant individuals, and people with inflammation.

medical.title: Gut microbiome features predict devastating disease affecting preemies
medical.summary: In a discovery that challenges long-standing assumptions about necrotizing enterocolitis, a sudden and often fatal intestinal illness that affects premature infants, researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis have identified previously unknown predictors for the disease.

medical.title: Ancestral diet-inspired pregnancy trial boosts growth in key fetal brain region
medical.summary: A nutrition program for pregnant women inspired by ancestral dietary patterns and adapted to locally available foods in Ecuador increased growth in a key fetal brain region, according to a study led by researchers at Washington University in St. Louis. The study is published in the Sept. 8 issue of the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

medical.title: The compounding problem of peptides
medical.summary: What if you could heal like Wolverine?

medical.title: Social media spreading misleading claims about Alzheimer's blood tests
medical.summary: Researchers are raising concerns about the promotion of Alzheimer's disease blood tests on social media, particularly posts making claims that do not align with current clinical recommendations. In the first published study of its kind, researchers from the University of Sydney analyzed 188 posts shared between March 2014 and May 2025 on Facebook, Instagram and TikTok about Alzheimer's blood tests, which have been allowed in Australia since July this year. Posts came from accounts with a combined audience of more than 114 million followers.

medical.title: Scientists find the whole grain “sweet spot” for better heart health
medical.summary: Eating four to six servings of whole grains a day may deliver meaningful benefits for heart health, according to a large review of 87 clinical trials. Researchers found improvements in body weight, waist size, blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, triglycerides, and some markers of inflammation.

medical.title: Scientists recreated what mice saw from brain activity alone
medical.summary: Scientists reconstructed videos from the brain activity of mice, producing 10-second clips based only on signals from neurons in the visual cortex. The breakthrough could help reveal how the brain reshapes what we see before it becomes our perception of reality.

medical.title: Scientists find a hidden retinal defense against vision loss
medical.summary: A naturally occurring molecule called erucamide may help the retina fight back against diseases that cause progressive vision loss. Restoring the molecule activated protective immune responses that helped stabilize retinal tissue and slow aspects of degeneration in preclinical models.

science.title: Hedgehog coronaviruses may threaten cats more than humans, new study finds
science.summary: Washington State University researchers have discovered how a group of coronaviruses circulating in hedgehogs invades host cells, a key to understanding their potential to jump between species and their risk of causing a pandemic in humans.

science.title: From 10 to 22 years: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's mission has just been extended
science.summary: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope hasn't yet reached its Sun–Earth L2 orbit, and it already has some good news. NASA has announced that the mission has enough fuel to potentially double its mission length. Though initially scheduled for five years of observations, followed by a five-year extended mission, the entire mission could now reach 22 years.

science.title: Toilet pellets may help us flush less and save water
science.summary: A pellet that dissolves in the toilet, turning the water blue and masking odor after urinating, could help us all save water, according to a first-of-its-kind study from the University of Surrey.

science.title: Gaming the market: Research provides insights for board game industry
science.summary: Anyone who has ever damaged a friendship over a supposedly friendly game of Monopoly knows the allure of board games.

science.title: Predominantly online friendships linked to greater support for white nationalism
science.summary: From social media to the streets of Washington, D.C., the organized white nationalist movement has become more visible in the United States over the past few decades. But the extent of this extremist movement's appeal to the broader public is less certain.

science.title: Land use and management intensity affect the suitability of habitats for wildlife in Europe
science.summary: Common, wide-ranging vertebrate species, such as foxes, may be finding more suitable habitat in towns and cities than in the wider landscape, while rarer species—which live in smaller areas—appear to favor different habitats, according to new research into species across Europe.

science.title: Ice Age carvers used mammoth tusk patterns to create unique art, study finds
science.summary: Intricate designs engraved across the surface of 18,000-year-old female figurines carved from mammoth ivory were inspired by the distinctive growth patterns visible in the tusks, a new study published in the journal npj Heritage Science has revealed.

science.title: Spring-like porous crystals could enable chemically responsive microscale materials
science.summary: Crystals are usually imagined as rigid objects with flat faces and straight edges. A research team led by the University of Osaka has recently created a porous crystal that grows into a spring-like helix. The team also found that the crystal can change shape as solvent molecules move in and out of its internal spaces. Their findings are published in Angewandte Chemie International Edition.

science.title: Some governments may hide a budget surplus to justify a tax hike
science.summary: It's annual property tax collection season, and with it may come questions about how those property taxes are used and, if there's a tax increase, why.

science.title: NASA Watches Earth’s Weight, Finds Center of Mass
science.summary: Seasonal changes redistribute enough water around Earth to shift the planet’s center of mass back and forth by fractions of an inch relative to its geometric center. NASA scientists are on the case, tracking the oscillations because Earth’s center of mass is a crucial reference point for satellite navigation and elevation measurements. A team, led […]

science.title: A 6-nanometer vapor barrier insulates ice during rapid heating
science.summary: Put a drop of water into a very hot pan, and it can skitter across the surface on a cushion of vapor. This is known as the Leidenfrost effect. Now, scientists have observed a related phenomenon involving ice and an extremely hot surface—on a length scale of billionths of a meter (nanometers) and within billionths of a second (nanoseconds).

science.title: Climate change is putting the squeeze on the world's grapegrowers
science.summary: This year, the European summer has been sweltering. It is unprecedented in many ways, marked by extreme heat, drought and record-breaking fires. Across the continent, fires have consumed hundreds of homes and prompted the evacuation of thousands of people.

science.title: The science behind greener, healthier lawns
science.summary: A healthy, green lawn can be the envy of any neighborhood, but how does someone cultivate a yard like that? Assistant Professor of Ecosystem Science Amber Churchill has been getting her hands dirty and digging into the science behind it.

science.title: 3D scans reveal how lichen fungi grip algae across cell walls
science.summary: Lichens colonize trees and rocks all over the world. They are symbiotic communities between fungi and photosynthetically active green algae or cyanobacteria, in which both partners benefit from each other: The fungal partner relies on the algae for a supply of carbohydrates and, in return, it protects the algae from UV radiation and other environmental influences. The contact zone where the fungal cells and algal cells touch is crucial for transferring nutrients between the two symbiotic partners. Detailed investigations, particularly a three-dimensional understanding of this area between the cells, have been lacking until now.

science.title: Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau
science.summary: Anak Krakatau erupts ash and volcanic gases in this Sept. 5, 2026, image acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8. Eruptions are a regular occurrence at Anak Krakatau, a small volcano between the Indonesian islands of Java and Sumatra. Much of its activity remains relatively mild, but it occasionally puts on more […]

The first was taken on Aug. 30, 2026, at 9:56 a.m. local Mars time; the second was taken on Sep. 2, 2026, at 5:39 p.m. local Mars time. Those […]

science.title: Pufferfish taste receptor more versatile than a human's, detecting both savory L- and sweet D-amino acids
science.summary: Our sense of taste is critical for survival, alerting us to substances that provide vital nutrients and those that might poison us. Now, a team led by researchers from the University of Osaka has discovered how one such taste receptor in pufferfish can detect a surprisingly wide range of flavors at once. Their study is published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

science.title: When equity appeals inspire giving to classrooms, what they signal matters
science.summary: Online crowdfunding platforms have enabled teachers in great need of classroom supplies to reach potential donors far beyond their school communities. Yet access to more donors does not automatically eliminate the disparities that shape which projects receive funding.

science.title: How some cyclists paradoxically start 'from rest' with a non-zero velocity
science.summary: Some track cyclists appear to break the rules of physics, but a new study, published in the journal Royal Society Open Science, has created a model explaining the illusion. The results suggest that a quick succession of well-timed moves can help cyclists get a head start without actually breaking the rules of the race or the rules of physics.

science.title: NASA Astronaut Reid Wiseman to Join NFL Fans in Baltimore
science.summary: As part of NASA’s new Inspiration Tour, Reid Wiseman, NASA astronaut and commander of the agency’s Artemis II mission, will highlight America’s strengths in space exploration and aeronautics innovation at the Baltimore Ravens vs. New Orleans Saints game in Baltimore on Sunday, Sept. 20. A Baltimore native, Wiseman is a 27-year Navy veteran and NASA […]

science.title: Measuring milk's carbon footprint
science.summary: Every product or service has a "carbon footprint," a measure of the environmental impact of creating or delivering it.

science.title: Half-billion-year-old fossils rewrite the origin story of starfish
science.summary: Scientists have discovered several 518-million-year-old fossils that reshape understanding of the origins of the animal group containing starfish. The fossils show that these animals ate using tentacles rather than passively using their gills, as previously thought.

science.title: NASA’s Integrated Medical Model (IMM)
science.summary: Planning crewed missions to the Moon and Mars involves preparing for the medical realities of long-duration space travel. Factors like cosmic radiation, microgravity, and distance from Earth create unique health considerations for astronauts. To anticipate these needs ahead of time, NASA developed the Integrated Medical Model (IMM). The IMM is a decision-support tool that uses […]

science.title: Scientists turn seawater into fresh water without harmful brine
science.summary: Scientists have developed a solar-powered desalination system that turns seawater into fresh water while removing nearly all of the leftover salt as a solid instead of producing harmful brine. The self-cleaning technology could also recover valuable minerals such as lithium, potentially turning desalination waste into a useful resource.

science.title: Quantitative training overhaul needed in ecology
science.summary: Ecologists are collecting more data than ever before, but many still lack confidence in the quantitative skills needed to make sense of it, according to a new paper.

environment.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
environment.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

environment.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
environment.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

environment.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

environment.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
environment.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.summary: Legea care prevede condițiile pentru acordarea alocațiilor pentru copii s-ar putea schimba. Un proiect aflat acum în dezbatere condiționează suma primită de prezența la școală a copilului. Cei care merg la ore și au nota 10 la purtare ar putea primi 60 de lei în plus în fiecare lună. În schimb, cei care chiulesc ar avea alocațiile reduse la 100 de lei. Legea a stârnit deja controverse.

mix_items.title: „Nici măcar nu știam că Liberia există”. Migranți din America Latină, deportați de SUA în Africa, la mii de kilometri de casă
mix_items.summary: Mai mulți migranți din America Latină au fost deportați de autoritățile americane în Liberia, o țară din Africa de Vest despre care unii dintre ei nici măcar nu știau că există. Aflați la mii de kilometri de familiile rămase în Statele Unite, aceștia spun că se simt blocați „în cealaltă parte a lumii” și se tem să revină în țările de origine, unde ar putea fi persecutați, potrivit CBS News.

mix_items.summary: Washington State University researchers have discovered how a group of coronaviruses circulating in hedgehogs invades host cells, a key to understanding their potential to jump between species and their risk of causing a pandemic in humans.

mix_items.title: From 10 to 22 years: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's mission has just been extended
mix_items.summary: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope hasn't yet reached its Sun–Earth L2 orbit, and it already has some good news. NASA has announced that the mission has enough fuel to potentially double its mission length. Though initially scheduled for five years of observations, followed by a five-year extended mission, the entire mission could now reach 22 years.

mix_items.summary: A pellet that dissolves in the toilet, turning the water blue and masking odor after urinating, could help us all save water, according to a first-of-its-kind study from the University of Surrey.

mix_items.title: Japanese hinoki root essential oil may support better sleep at home
mix_items.summary: Sleep problems are common in middle age, particularly among women in their 40s and 50s. In a new study published Sept. 1, 2026, in the Journal of Wood Science, researchers explored whether essential oils derived from Hinoki (Chamaecyparis obtusa), known as Japanese cypress, roots could help improve sleep quality. Participants reported fewer nighttime awakenings, improved morning feelings and brain-wave patterns suggesting smoother sleep onset.

mix_items.title: Gaming the market: Research provides insights for board game industry
mix_items.summary: Anyone who has ever damaged a friendship over a supposedly friendly game of Monopoly knows the allure of board games.

mix_items.title: New mechanism reveals how atypical E. coli maintain their ability to infect
mix_items.summary: A new study shows how a type of disease-causing E. coli can quickly adapt when it loses one of its main ways of attaching to the intestine. The bacteria either change shape or make small changes to a protein that strengthens their grip on human cells. The findings help explain why these strains can still cause illness and identify a possible target for future treatments that could stop infection by preventing bacteria from attaching in the first place.

mix_items.title: Predominantly online friendships linked to greater support for white nationalism
mix_items.summary: From social media to the streets of Washington, D.C., the organized white nationalist movement has become more visible in the United States over the past few decades. But the extent of this extremist movement's appeal to the broader public is less certain.

mix_items.title: Three studies map how superbugs evade antibiotics and spread to vulnerable patients
mix_items.summary: To defeat multidrug-resistant superbugs, bacterial defenses must be confronted wherever they may emerge, from basic genetic mutations in a laboratory to complex real-world transmission in hospital rooms. A new trio of studies published in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy and researched by the laboratory of Barry N. Kreiswirth, Ph.D., at the Hackensack Meridian Center for Discovery and Innovation (CDI) demonstrates how an integrated approach might yet expose and overcome these diverse survival mechanisms.

mix_items.title: Land use and management intensity affect the suitability of habitats for wildlife in Europe
mix_items.summary: Common, wide-ranging vertebrate species, such as foxes, may be finding more suitable habitat in towns and cities than in the wider landscape, while rarer species—which live in smaller areas—appear to favor different habitats, according to new research into species across Europe.

mix_items.title: Ice Age carvers used mammoth tusk patterns to create unique art, study finds
mix_items.summary: Intricate designs engraved across the surface of 18,000-year-old female figurines carved from mammoth ivory were inspired by the distinctive growth patterns visible in the tusks, a new study published in the journal npj Heritage Science has revealed.

mix_items.title: Study reveals young-onset dementia's impact on families
mix_items.summary: Families caring for a loved one with young-onset dementia are facing years of uncertainty, financial strain and emotional exhaustion—with many struggling to access timely diagnosis and appropriate support—according to a new Curtin University study appearing in Health Expectations.

mix_items.title: Osteoporosis fractures fall by 94% in small first-in-human stem cell trial
mix_items.summary: Somewhere in the world, a woman over 50 will have fractured a bone by the time you finish reading this sentence due to osteoporosis, a silent bone disease that can weaken the structural integrity of the skeletal system and a person's quality of life. The disease weakens bones and makes them more likely to break because of reduced bone mineral density and bone mass, and it affects an estimated 75 million people across Europe, the USA, and Japan.

mix_items.title: Spring-like porous crystals could enable chemically responsive microscale materials
mix_items.summary: Crystals are usually imagined as rigid objects with flat faces and straight edges. A research team led by the University of Osaka has recently created a porous crystal that grows into a spring-like helix. The team also found that the crystal can change shape as solvent molecules move in and out of its internal spaces. Their findings are published in Angewandte Chemie International Edition.

mix_items.title: Some governments may hide a budget surplus to justify a tax hike
mix_items.summary: It's annual property tax collection season, and with it may come questions about how those property taxes are used and, if there's a tax increase, why.

mix_items.title: Emergency department visits for gambling disorders nearly doubled after Ontario expanded its online gambling market
mix_items.summary: Emergency department (ED) visits for gambling disorders doubled following the legalization of single-event sports betting and expansion of Ontario's online gambling market, according to a new study from ICES. The increase was observed predominantly among young men.

mix_items.title: NASA Watches Earth’s Weight, Finds Center of Mass
mix_items.summary: Seasonal changes redistribute enough water around Earth to shift the planet’s center of mass back and forth by fractions of an inch relative to its geometric center. NASA scientists are on the case, tracking the oscillations because Earth’s center of mass is a crucial reference point for satellite navigation and elevation measurements. A team, led […]

mix_items.title: A 6-nanometer vapor barrier insulates ice during rapid heating
mix_items.summary: Put a drop of water into a very hot pan, and it can skitter across the surface on a cushion of vapor. This is known as the Leidenfrost effect. Now, scientists have observed a related phenomenon involving ice and an extremely hot surface—on a length scale of billionths of a meter (nanometers) and within billionths of a second (nanoseconds).

mix_items.title: Study supports effectiveness of RSV preventive antibodies for infants, offers new way to monitor viral resistance
mix_items.summary: An analysis of more than 60,000 respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) sequences from around the world found that viral variants associated with resistance to current RSV prevention tools remain rare, according to a study published in Nature.

mix_items.title: Climate change is putting the squeeze on the world's grapegrowers
mix_items.summary: This year, the European summer has been sweltering. It is unprecedented in many ways, marked by extreme heat, drought and record-breaking fires. Across the continent, fires have consumed hundreds of homes and prompted the evacuation of thousands of people.

mix_items.title: The science behind greener, healthier lawns
mix_items.summary: A healthy, green lawn can be the envy of any neighborhood, but how does someone cultivate a yard like that? Assistant Professor of Ecosystem Science Amber Churchill has been getting her hands dirty and digging into the science behind it.

mix_items.title: 3D scans reveal how lichen fungi grip algae across cell walls
mix_items.summary: Lichens colonize trees and rocks all over the world. They are symbiotic communities between fungi and photosynthetically active green algae or cyanobacteria, in which both partners benefit from each other: The fungal partner relies on the algae for a supply of carbohydrates and, in return, it protects the algae from UV radiation and other environmental influences. The contact zone where the fungal cells and algal cells touch is crucial for transferring nutrients between the two symbiotic partners. Detailed investigations, particularly a three-dimensional understanding of this area between the cells, have been lacking until now.

mix_items.title: New study reveals how a brain protein may influence ADHD and brain development
mix_items.summary: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that can affect attention, activity levels and impulse control, with symptoms often beginning in childhood and sometimes continuing into adulthood.

mix_items.title: Targeting Nav1.7: A new approach to long-lasting relief from nerve pain
mix_items.summary: Pain is a natural protective mechanism that alerts the body to actual or potential injury. But when nerves themselves are damaged, they can generate abnormal pain signals even in the absence of a new injury. This condition, known as neuropathic pain, can be persistent and difficult to treat. Medicines can sometimes provide inadequate relief or cause unwanted effects, creating a need for treatments that can reduce abnormal pain without interfering with normal pain sensation.

mix_items.title: Pufferfish taste receptor more versatile than a human's, detecting both savory L- and sweet D-amino acids
mix_items.summary: Our sense of taste is critical for survival, alerting us to substances that provide vital nutrients and those that might poison us. Now, a team led by researchers from the University of Osaka has discovered how one such taste receptor in pufferfish can detect a surprisingly wide range of flavors at once. Their study is published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

mix_items.title: When equity appeals inspire giving to classrooms, what they signal matters
mix_items.summary: Online crowdfunding platforms have enabled teachers in great need of classroom supplies to reach potential donors far beyond their school communities. Yet access to more donors does not automatically eliminate the disparities that shape which projects receive funding.

mix_items.title: How some cyclists paradoxically start 'from rest' with a non-zero velocity
mix_items.summary: Some track cyclists appear to break the rules of physics, but a new study, published in the journal Royal Society Open Science, has created a model explaining the illusion. The results suggest that a quick succession of well-timed moves can help cyclists get a head start without actually breaking the rules of the race or the rules of physics.

mix_items.summary: As part of NASA’s new Inspiration Tour, Reid Wiseman, NASA astronaut and commander of the agency’s Artemis II mission, will highlight America’s strengths in space exploration and aeronautics innovation at the Baltimore Ravens vs. New Orleans Saints game in Baltimore on Sunday, Sept. 20. A Baltimore native, Wiseman is a 27-year Navy veteran and NASA […]

mix_items.title: Can psychedelic clinical trials be better? Researchers say yes
mix_items.summary: UC San Francisco researchers are weighing in on one of the biggest challenges in psychedelic science, arguing that clinical trials need more convincing placebo treatments to better measure the drugs' true effects.

mix_items.title: New portable blood testing device could allow patient health to be monitored at home through an app
mix_items.summary: King's College London spinout Algocyte has developed a small blood-testing device that connects via Bluetooth and uses AI to build a picture of an individual's health over time. The tool could be especially beneficial for patients who require regular monitoring, such as those undergoing chemotherapy, who currently rely on frequent hospital or doctor visits for blood tests.

mix_items.title: Measuring milk's carbon footprint
mix_items.summary: Every product or service has a "carbon footprint," a measure of the environmental impact of creating or delivering it.

mix_items.title: Half-billion-year-old fossils rewrite the origin story of starfish
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered several 518-million-year-old fossils that reshape understanding of the origins of the animal group containing starfish. The fossils show that these animals ate using tentacles rather than passively using their gills, as previously thought.

mix_items.title: NASA’s Integrated Medical Model (IMM)
mix_items.summary: Planning crewed missions to the Moon and Mars involves preparing for the medical realities of long-duration space travel. Factors like cosmic radiation, microgravity, and distance from Earth create unique health considerations for astronauts. To anticipate these needs ahead of time, NASA developed the Integrated Medical Model (IMM). The IMM is a decision-support tool that uses […]

mix_items.title: Scientists turn seawater into fresh water without harmful brine
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed a solar-powered desalination system that turns seawater into fresh water while removing nearly all of the leftover salt as a solid instead of producing harmful brine. The self-cleaning technology could also recover valuable minerals such as lithium, potentially turning desalination waste into a useful resource.

mix_items.title: Quantitative training overhaul needed in ecology
mix_items.summary: Ecologists are collecting more data than ever before, but many still lack confidence in the quantitative skills needed to make sense of it, according to a new paper.

mix_items.title: Hope in the Storm: Studying the Daily Fight to Live
mix_items.summary: Understanding and preventing suicide often focuses on why people want to die—but a Yale researcher is calling for a shift to a more constructive, humanizing starting point. Christine Cha, PhD, stresses the importance of focusing on why many people who feel suicidal keep trying to live.

mix_items.title: Wearable sensors accurately track knee osteoarthritis mobility
mix_items.summary: Knee osteoarthritis is a widespread and painful joint condition. It causes chronic pain, cartilage breakdown and trouble moving. Doctors rely on X-rays and patient surveys to track how the disease progresses. These traditional methods have a major blind spot. They do not show how a person actually moves during daily life outside a clinical exam.

mix_items.title: Clinical guideline on radiation therapy for bladder cancer released
mix_items.summary: For appropriately selected patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer, preserving the bladder can be a curative treatment option rather than removing it, according to a new clinical guideline from the American Society for Radiation Oncology (ASTRO). The recommendations support trimodal therapy as an alternative to bladder removal and provide guidance on the use of radiation therapy after surgery and for patients with metastatic or symptomatic disease. The guideline, ASTRO's first to focus specifically on radiation therapy across bladder cancer care, was published in Practical Radiation Oncology, ASTRO's clinical practice journal.

mix_items.title: Gut supplement shows promise against opioid-related damage in rat pups
mix_items.summary: New UNSW research published in Translational Psychiatry shows a gut supplement can repair opioid-related damage in rat pups, raising hopes for a future treatment for babies exposed to opioids in the womb.

mix_items.title: Caregivers worldwide often sacrifice their own well-being, 20 years of research further confirms
mix_items.summary: Caregivers of people with cancer, heart problems and other long-term illnesses report needing more psychological support but often stop short of accessing it.

mix_items.title: Scientists find an immune “false alarm” that may drive rapid aging
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that some severe genetic disorders linked to rapid aging may be driven not just by damaged DNA, but by the body’s overreaction to that damage. When broken DNA fragments leak into the wrong part of a cell, an immune sensor called cGAS can mistake them for signs of a viral infection, triggering chronic inflammation and even interfering with DNA repair itself.

mix_items.title: ASH sets new standards for diagnosing iron deficiency
mix_items.summary: Iron deficiency is one of the most common health conditions in the world, but many people live with symptoms for months or years before receiving a diagnosis. To address this critical unmet need, the American Society of Hematology (ASH) issued new clinical guidance to improve how iron deficiency is recognized and diagnosed across key populations, including adults, young children, menstruating and pregnant individuals, and people with inflammation.

mix_items.title: Gut microbiome features predict devastating disease affecting preemies
mix_items.summary: In a discovery that challenges long-standing assumptions about necrotizing enterocolitis, a sudden and often fatal intestinal illness that affects premature infants, researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis have identified previously unknown predictors for the disease.

mix_items.title: Ancestral diet-inspired pregnancy trial boosts growth in key fetal brain region
mix_items.summary: A nutrition program for pregnant women inspired by ancestral dietary patterns and adapted to locally available foods in Ecuador increased growth in a key fetal brain region, according to a study led by researchers at Washington University in St. Louis. The study is published in the Sept. 8 issue of the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

mix_items.summary: What if you could heal like Wolverine?

mix_items.title: Social media spreading misleading claims about Alzheimer's blood tests
mix_items.summary: Researchers are raising concerns about the promotion of Alzheimer's disease blood tests on social media, particularly posts making claims that do not align with current clinical recommendations. In the first published study of its kind, researchers from the University of Sydney analyzed 188 posts shared between March 2014 and May 2025 on Facebook, Instagram and TikTok about Alzheimer's blood tests, which have been allowed in Australia since July this year. Posts came from accounts with a combined audience of more than 114 million followers.

mix_items.title: Scientists find the whole grain “sweet spot” for better heart health
mix_items.summary: Eating four to six servings of whole grains a day may deliver meaningful benefits for heart health, according to a large review of 87 clinical trials. Researchers found improvements in body weight, waist size, blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, triglycerides, and some markers of inflammation.

mix_items.title: Scientists recreated what mice saw from brain activity alone
mix_items.summary: Scientists reconstructed videos from the brain activity of mice, producing 10-second clips based only on signals from neurons in the visual cortex. The breakthrough could help reveal how the brain reshapes what we see before it becomes our perception of reality.

mix_items.title: Scientists find a hidden retinal defense against vision loss
mix_items.summary: A naturally occurring molecule called erucamide may help the retina fight back against diseases that cause progressive vision loss. Restoring the molecule activated protective immune responses that helped stabilize retinal tissue and slow aspects of degeneration in preclinical models.

mix_items.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
mix_items.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

mix_items.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
mix_items.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

mix_items.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
mix_items.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
